title: The Lyapunov function $\Phi = \log_q |P|$ and the Hausdorff phase transition
html:
Remark. The Lyapunov function \Phi = \log_q |P| and the Hausdorff phase transition

The Hausdorff dimension recurrence (Hausdorff recurrence) provides the only universal convergence proof in this paper. The map q_{n+1} = (q_n^2 - q_n + 1)/q_n contracts for all q > 3/4, with q = 1 as a superattracting fixed point (F'(1) = 0). The q-Collatz conjecture shares a parallel structure, but with one critical difference.

The Lyapunov function \Phi = \log_q |P|

The natural Lyapunov function for the Skein-Collatz uses q as the logarithm base:

  \Phi(P)  :=  \log_q |P|.

Why q? Because the contraction gap is q itself: [2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q. The base-q logarithm converts this gap into unit decrease: when a cycle has v = 2 halvings, \Phi decreases by

  |\Delta\Phi|
  = 
  \log_q \frac{[2]_q^2}{[3]_q}
  = 
  \log_q\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{[3]_q}\right).

At q_0 = 1.109978595642739\ldots (muon pin, 16 dps): |\Delta\Phi| \approx 2.76 per cycle. An orbit starting at P with \Phi_0 = \log_q |P| reaches the fixed point \Phi = 0 (i.e., P = 1) after \Phi_0 / |\Delta\Phi| cycles.

Entropy cost of convergence

Each Collatz cycle with v = 2 halvings consists of 3 Reeb steps (1 odd + 2 even), each consuming \eta_q = (2q-1)/q^3 q-bits of operational entropy (operational entropy). The total entropy budget to convergence is:

  I_{\mathrm{total}}
  = 
  \frac{\Phi_0}{|\Delta\Phi|} \cdot 3\eta_q
   \approx 
  \Phi_0 \cdot \eta_q
  \quad q\text{-bits}.

At q_0, converging from |P| = 1000 costs about 65 q-bits — roughly 24 Collatz cycles, each consuming \sim 2.7 q-bits. The orbit is an information-bounded computation: it processes a finite, predictable amount of entropy before terminating.

The discrete phase transition at v = 2

The Hausdorff recurrence is smooth: the derivative F'(q) = 1 - 1/q^2 varies continuously, reaching 0 at the fixed point (superattraction). The orbit decelerates as it approaches q = 1 — each step costs more entropy but covers less distance.

The Collatz contraction is discrete: the valuation v \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\} is an integer, and the threshold v^* \in (1, 2) falls between two integers. There is no gradual approach. The contraction ratio jumps:

  R(v) = \frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^v}:
  \qquad
  R(1) \approx \tfrac{3}{2} > 1,
  \qquad
  R(2) \approx \tfrac{3}{4} < 1,
  \qquad
  R(3) \approx \tfrac{3}{8} < 1.

This is a discrete phase transition: below v = 2 the orbit expands, at v = 2 it contracts by 3/4, and at v \geq 3 it contracts even faster. There is no critical slowing-down and no superattraction.

Implications for the conjecture

The Hausdorff recurrence converges unconditionally because F'(q) < 1 for all q > 3/4 — the derivative is negative everywhere in the physical range, so every orbit enters the basin of the superattracting fixed point.

The Collatz dynamics converge conditionally: the contraction R(2) < 1 fires only when v \geq 2. The conjecture asks whether every orbit produces v \geq 2 often enough. The algebra guarantees that v = 2 suffices ([2]^2 > [3], gap = q); the no-periodic-cycles theorem (no cycles) eliminates the main alternative to convergence; and the classical average \mathbb{E}[v_2] = 2 saturates the threshold.

Connection via Planck steps

Both the Hausdorff recurrence and the Collatz cycle advance by Planck-scale steps. The Hausdorff map uses \delta q = \hbar_q as the step size (one Reeb phase advance in q-space). The Collatz cycle consumes n_R(q) = q/(q-1) Reeb iterations (operations per Planck).

The Hausdorff step and the Collatz Lyapunov step are commensurate:

  \frac{|\Delta\Phi|}{\hbar_q}
  = 
  \frac{\log_q([2]^2/[3])}{(q-1)/q}
   \approx  2.9
  \quad\text{at } q_0.

Each Collatz cycle (at v = 2) covers about 3 Planck steps worth of Lyapunov decrease. The Collatz orbit is a discrete walk on the same parameter space that the Hausdorff recurrence traverses smoothly, both using the substrate parameter as their natural scale.
